extracted.intended_audience: literate public interested in literature, theatre, wit, and social/taste criticism (writers, actors, theatregoers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for theatrical writing, acting, conversational wit, and public decorum as argued in Spectator essays—what makes stage works, comic devices, and public behaviour tasteful or offensive. Useful for writing for the stage, composing allegory, or judging wit and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the finest Compositions among the Ancients are in Allegory; the author has endeavoured to revive that way of Writing and finds there is always a great Demand for those particular Papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory is a respected, high form of composition with public demand. Use personification and symbolic structure (as in the Vision pieces) to explore passions and moral themes; the form can be revived successfully for contemporary readers. Example: the author's own Vision-of-Grief allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage should respect common sense and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stage often moves people against all common Sense and Humanity; good stage-work should not provoke reactions contrary to humane sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes that make an audience take pleasure in another's genuine suffering or in actions that violate basic decency. Anti-pattern example: an old woman's real pain being clapped off the stage for laughter. Use empathy and humane depiction rather than spectacle of suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as a picture of human life with worthy sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedy may be a 'perfect Picture of human Life' and still not raise cheap Laughter—refined comedy pleases by sober, polite mirth and worthy sentiments rather than bawdy sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for natural, truthful characterisation and sentiments that display humanity and elegance rather than relying on coarse jokes. Example: Terence's 'Self-Tormentor' pleases a refined audience despite little overt laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reception as a barometer of public disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: What passes on the Stage, and the Reception it meets with from the Audience, is a very useful Instruction of this Kind [to judge the people's dispositions].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and critics should read audience reaction to understand prevailing tastes and moral temperament. Statesmen may use this to judge how to address the public. Use reception as evidence but beware conflating noisy approval with true merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors must serve the author's words (no ad-libbing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intolerable Folly and Confidence of Players putting in Words of their own feeds the absurd Taste of the Audience; an actor who inserts or substitutes lines harms both play and public taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage actors from adding improvised lines or mannerisms that overshadow the author's text. Good acting should highlight the author's sentiments and naturalness rather than personal flourishes that distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage material must not be offensive to virtue or good manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is required to have an immediate Tendency to the Promotion of Virtue, but representations should not be against the Interests of Virtue, nor offensive to Good-manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works may be morally neutral, but should avoid endorsing vice or shocking decency. Use discretion with sexual or violent material; well-drawn neutral or comic scenes are acceptable when they do not undermine virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-drawn rusticities and character touches are acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no Exception to the well-drawn Rusticities in the Country-Wake; such touches (e.g., Dogget's Hob) are miraculously pleasant and welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rustic characters and vividly observed rural comic details are legitimate and enjoyable elements of stage-writing when handled skilfully. Example: Dogget's comic portrayal praised despite other objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spectacle and violence as the primary source of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent touches and the justest Pictures of human Life pass by like mere narration while the height of the Jest is often in the point that Heads are broken or spectacle is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on noisy spectacle, staged violence, or gross physicality to obtain laughs; such techniques distract from subtler comic craft and cater to the lower appetites of the pit/audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning and mechanical exercises are inferior wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning and mechanical games (cross-purposes, crambo, cap Verses) are exercises for those wanting Wit but of small Intellects; they substitute mechanical tricks for genuine wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer original, thoughtful humour over formulaic wordplay and mechanical verse tricks. While these amusements have a place, they do not suffice for a gentleman's ordinary discourse or for sustained comic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecent double meanings and ill-bred allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some persons, to supply want of Wit, harp upon things they ought not to allude to and deal mighty in double Meanings—these offend, especially women, and display want of breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from low, sexual innuendo or crude double entendres in polite company or stage works aimed at decent audiences. Such devices flatter coarse tastes and alienate well-bred listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'biting' as deceitful wit
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Biter' tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve, then cries 'Bite' and triumphs at having deceived you; depending upon deceit for wit is knavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tricks that rely on misleading an interlocutor for the sake of a punchline; this form of wit (biting) is dishonest and pernicious. Example anecdote: a false report of a man's father's death revealed as a 'bite'—cruel and unbecoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors and players should prefer applause of the reasonable audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Players who prefer the Applause of Fools to that of the reasonable part of the Company are blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers and authors should aim to please the intelligent, discerning portion of the audience rather than courting the cheap approval of noisy, unthinking spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public decorum: avoid ostentation in sacred/public spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Glaring and ostentatious Behaviour, even in laudable things, should be discountenanced in sacred places; those who come to give themselves 'airs' in church disturb the devotion of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In depiction and in social conduct, show respect for religious settings; characters or real persons who use sacred gatherings to display themselves are portrayed as disruptive and deserving of censure (example: the 'Phantom' at church). This is a standard for social taste and for realistic, moral characterisation.
